newsitem.title: USA: FBI, Civil Rights Commission to probe St. Pete riot.
newsitem.headline: FBI, Civil Rights Commission to probe St. Pete riot.

text.p: A team from the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights was in this Florida city Wednesday to assess race relations after rioting provoked by the killing of a black youth by a white police officer, a commission spokesman said.
The FBI has also announced it will launch an investigation of police conduct in the shooting death of Tyron Lewis, 18, last Thursday.
The rioting in the poor black neighbourhood of South St.Petersburg lasted into the early hours of Friday morning and prompted the city mayor to declare a state of emergency, lifted on Sunday.
At least 11 people were hurt, mostly police officers, and nearly 30 fires set in shops, businesses and homes before police regained control.

Black youths complained they were constantly victimised by police and community leaders said poverty, lack of jobs and bleak prospects for blacks in St.Petersburg created a resentment which fuelled the unrest.

The head of the Civil Rights Commission, Mary Frances Berry, and other commission officials were in St. Petersburg to talk to city officials and members of the community, spokesman Charles Rivera said.

Berry plans to set up a Florida Advisory Committee within 30 days to gather information. A similar forum in 1993 found racial tensions arising from police treatment but the advisory committee later reported finding improvement.
The Justice Department said Deval Patrick, assistant attorney general for civil rights, would work with the FBI on a "complete and independent" investigation into the incident.

Lewis was shot at the wheel of his car by police officer James Knight after he was stopped for speeding. Knight said Lewis appeared to lunge the car forward in an effort to run him and his colleague down.
Patrick met city officials including Police Chief Darrel Stephens and church and black leaders in St.Petersburg Tuesday, the Justice Department said in a statement.
Lewis' funeral is due to take place Saturday, which mayor David Fischer has described as a "critical time" because of the possibility of renewed unrest.
